input:
The affinity laws are a set of simple yet powerful relationships that allow us to predict how the performance of a centrifugal pump will change when its operating speed is varied. Taken together, the laws consist of three proportionalities that link the main performance quantities to the rotational speed. First of all, the flow delivered by the pump is directly proportional to the speed, so that any change in speed produces the same proportional change in flow. Secondly, the head developed by the pump is proportional to the square of the speed, meaning that the head responds much more strongly to a speed change than the flow does. Thirdly, and most dramatically, the power absorbed by the pump is proportional to the cube of the speed, making power by far the most sensitive of the three quantities.

A simple worked check helps to make these relationships concrete. Suppose that the speed of the pump is doubled. The flow will simply double, in line with the first proportionality. The head, however, will rise fourfold, because the square of a doubled speed is four times the original value. The power, following the cube law, will increase by a factor of 8, a striking illustration of how expensive additional flow becomes when it is obtained by raising the speed. Conversely, even a modest reduction in speed can deliver a disproportionately large saving in power. It should be remembered that these laws relate the operating points of one and the same pump handling one and the same fluid, and that they describe what the pump offers at the new speed rather than the duty point that the surrounding system will ultimately settle at.
target:
The affinity laws relate the performance of a centrifugal pump at one speed to the performance of the same pump at another speed. Three proportionalities hold. The flow is proportional to the speed. The head is proportional to the square of the speed. The power is proportional to the cube of the speed.

A worked check fixes the meaning of the three laws at one speed change. Double the speed. The flow doubles, because the flow follows the speed directly. The head rises fourfold, because the head follows the square of the speed, and the square of a doubled quantity is four times the original. The power rises by the cube of the speed ratio: a doubled speed multiplies the power by 8.

The check states the practical weight of the laws. Flow is bought with power at a steep rate, because the power grows with the cube of the speed while the flow grows only in direct proportion. The relation runs in reverse with the same force: a small reduction in speed removes a much larger share of the power than of the flow. The laws relate the operating points of one pump on one fluid to each other. They state nothing about the system the pump serves, and a point fixed by the laws is the pump's offering at the new speed, not the duty the system will settle at.
